From Avinguda Diagonal the road tilts up within a kilometre and then simply refuses to let go. This loop works the Serra de Collserola — the wooded ridge of holm oak and pine wedged between Barcelona and the Vallès plain — from three different sides, and the numbers show it: 1,398 m of climbing in 63 km, only 12% of the distance genuinely flat, and 44% of it pointing downhill. The first sustained effort runs up the Llobregat flank past Can Calopa to the Romanesque church at Santa Creu d’Olorda and over Coll de Can Mallol. The second is the short, sharp haul to Tibidabo at 504 m — the high point of the ride and of the city. The loop then drops north into Sant Cugat, crosses the plain at Bellaterra and Cerdanyola, and climbs the ridge a third time past the Iberian settlement of Ca n’Oliver before the long descent through Horta returns you to city tarmac. Steep and technical throughout, and never more than twenty minutes from a café.

On the road

Surfaces are good but the Collserola descents are narrow, gravel-strewn in places and busy with walkers and runners at weekends. The Tibidabo road closes to through traffic at times for the funicular and amusement park — check before committing. Water at Vallvidrera and at the Tibidabo summit; nothing between Olorda and Molins de Rei.

Points of interest

km 10.1

Vil·la Joana, Vallvidrera

A 19th-century country house on the col above Vallvidrera, now a museum to the poet Jacint Verdaguer, who died here in 1902. It sits beside the Romanesque church of Santa Maria de Vallvidrera at the point where the climb out of Sarrià finally levels off — the traditional place to stop and look back over the city.

km 23.1

Santa Creu d’Olorda

A pre-Romanesque church first documented in the 10th century, standing at a junction of ridge roads with the ruins of Castell d’Olorda just above. It marks the top of the long western climb and the start of the traverse along the spine of Collserola.

km 30.4

Torre de Collserola

Norman Foster’s 288-metre communications tower, built for the 1992 Olympics and visible from most of the Barcelona plain. The road passes directly beneath it a kilometre before Tibidabo, on the steepest kilometre of the whole loop (8.4% average).

km 31.6

Temple Expiatori del Sagrat Cor

The neo-Gothic church that crowns Tibidabo at 504 m, begun in 1902 and finished in 1961, with a bronze Christ on its topmost spire. Next door is the Parc d’Atraccions, open since 1905 and still running its original aeroplane ride — this is the summit of the ride.

km 45.9

Poblat ibèric de Ca n’Oliver

An Iberian hilltop settlement occupied from roughly the 6th to the 1st century BC, excavated and partly reconstructed above Cerdanyola. It sits at the foot of the final climb back over the ridge, on the Vallès side where the loop turns for home.

The wild one. Starting inland among the Penedès vineyards at Sant Pere Molanta, the route drives straight into the limestone heart of the Parc Natural del Garraf — a karst massif of bare white rock, dwarf palm and garrigue that looks closer to North Africa than to the Mediterranean coast three kilometres away. The interior road climbs in three steps past the Buddhist monastery at La Plana Novella to the Collada de Vallgrassa, which delivers the single steepest pitch on any of these four routes: 17% over 200 m. A ridge traverse past the Pla de Querol mirador tops out at 477 m before the Rat Penat road drops you to the sea at Sitges. The coast strip to Castelldefels is the only easy part; the long pull back over Begues and Olesa de Bonesvalls to the Penedès closes the loop. Shadeless, exposed and almost waterless once you leave Olivella — carry more than you think.

On the road

The least forgiving of the four. No shade, no shops and no reliable water between Olivella (km 5) and Sitges (km 29) — roughly 24 km and 550 m of climbing on a dry ridge. Do it early in the day or out of high summer. The Vallgrassa ramp is short but genuinely 17%; gear for it.

Points of interest

km 0

Sant Pere Molanta, Olèrdola

The start: a small Penedès village surrounded by vines, on the back road from Vilafranca towards Sant Pere de Ribes. Everything green and cultivated here disappears within eight kilometres as the route climbs into the limestone.

km 18

Sakya Tashi Ling, La Plana Novella

A Tibetan Buddhist monastery installed in the Palau Novella, a colonial-style mansion built in the 1880s by a returning Cuba emigrant in the middle of what is now the natural park. Its white stupa appears without warning in a fold of dry hills at the top of the first climb.

km 21.2

Collada de Vallgrassa

The hardest 200 metres on this page: 17% out of the Fondo de Vallgrassa, with the restored Vallgrassa farmhouse — now a contemporary art centre — on the shoulder above. Beyond it the road links a chain of cols at 400–420 m across the roof of the massif.

km 24.4

Mirador del Pla de Querol

A viewpoint at the route’s 477 m high point, looking across bare karst pavement, sinkholes and dwarf-palm scrub to the sea. The Garraf’s limestone drains so completely that there are no surface streams at all — which is why there is no water on this ridge.

km 29.5

Sitges seafront

The Rat Penat road drops 470 m to the Mediterranean and lands on the promenade at Sitges, the first shade, water and coffee in 25 km. From here the route runs flat along the coast to Castelldefels before turning inland for the long climb home.

A reconnaissance of the business end of the 2026 Tour de France’s second stage. The race itself runs 168.5 km from Tarragona with around 2,500 m of climbing, nearly all of it packed into the final 93 km; this ride picks that sequence up in Barcelona, rolls out flat across the Llobregat delta, and then rides the part that decides it — the Côte de Begues out of Gavà, the high traverse over Coll Carrascal and Coll del Corral above Olesa de Bonesvalls, the drop through Vallirana and Molins de Rei, and the Montjuïc finishing circuit, which this GPX laps twice and the race will lap three times. Two-fifths of the route is dead flat and a third of it is descending: it keeps its powder dry for 70 km, then asks the question with a two-kilometre wall averaging 7.6% and touching 13%.

On the road

The delta section uses cycle paths and service roads and is slow but safe; the Montjuïc circuit is open to traffic and the descent off the castle is steep with tight corners. Expect the flat first 70 km to feel much harder into a sea breeze than the profile suggests.

Points of interest

km 12

Delta del Llobregat

The flat opening threads the delta on cycle paths and service roads between the airport runways, market gardens and the Remolar-Filipines lagoons — a protected wetland and one of the best bird sites on the Catalan coast. Wind is the only resistance for 20 km.

km 21.4

Mines prehistòriques de Gavà

Right where the road tilts up out of Gavà: the oldest known underground mines in Europe, dug about 6,000 years ago to extract variscite, a green gemstone traded across the western Mediterranean. The visitor centre takes you down into a Neolithic shaft.

km 25.6

Castell d’Eramprunyà

Look left, mid-climb: a castle first recorded in the 10th century, perched on a red sandstone spur that commanded the whole coastal plain between the Llobregat and the Garraf. The Côte de Begues passes a couple of hundred metres below it.

km 39

Antic Hospital de Cervelló

A 13th-century pilgrims’ and travellers’ hospital founded by the Cervelló family on the old road from Barcelona to the Penedès, still standing largely intact at Olesa de Bonesvalls. The route passes its door at the foot of the climb to Coll Carrascal.

km 75.8

Castell de Montjuïc

The summit of the finishing climb, at 166 m on this GPX: an 18th-century fortress on the headland above the port, reached by a two-kilometre ramp averaging 7.6% and touching 13%. The race crosses it three times; this route does it twice.

The full day out, and the only route here that breaks 100 km. From the Vila Olímpica it runs the beaches to Castelldefels, turns inland at Gavà, and takes the long way up through Begues to the 413 m high point of the Garraf massif — nine kilometres of climbing that gains more height than any other single ascent on this page. Across the top of the park it reaches the Penedès edge at Coll de Garró, then drops through Olivella and Sant Pere de Ribes to Sitges. The reward is the way home: the C-31 Costes del Garraf, a corniche cut into the sea cliffs, with the Celler Güell standing at the roadside in Garraf hamlet. Nearly half the route is flat, so the day has a simple shape — one big climb in the first third, one long coastal roll home, and the wind gets to decide which of the two was harder.

On the road

The C-31 corniche is spectacular but it is a main road with tunnels and no shoulder in places — lights front and rear, and avoid Sunday evenings when Sitges empties back towards Barcelona. Sitges at km 76 is the obvious lunch stop and the last easy resupply before the coast road.

Points of interest

km 13

Platja de Castelldefels

Five kilometres of dune-backed beach with the Garraf massif rising straight out of the sea at the far end — the wall the route spends the next 20 km climbing over. Flat, fast, and completely exposed to whatever the sea breeze is doing.

km 50.7

Coll de Garró & the Penedès edge

At 231 m the route slips over the northern rim of the park and the landscape changes in a hundred metres: karst scrub gives way to the vineyards of the Alt Penedès, Catalonia’s cava country. It is the furthest point from the sea on the whole ride.

km 76.8

Sitges old town

The church of Sant Bartomeu i Santa Tecla stands on a rock over the beach, with the Maricel palace and the Cau Ferrat museum — the painter Santiago Rusiñol’s house — beside it. Halfway point, lunch stop, and the last easy resupply before the corniche.

km 88

Celler Güell, Garraf

A stone-and-tile wine cellar and gatehouse right on the coast road, built for Eusebi Güell around 1895; long attributed to Gaudí, it is now generally credited to his collaborator Francesc Berenguer. You pass within thirty metres of it.

km 95

Costes del Garraf

Twenty kilometres of corniche cut into the cliffs between Sitges and Castelldefels, with the railway in tunnels below and the massif rising vertically above. The best road on any of these four routes, and the reason to ride the loop in this direction.

How these numbers were made

Every figure comes from the four GPX files themselves. Each track was resampled onto a uniform 20 m grid and the elevation smoothed over a 200 m window before gradients were taken — without that step, GPS and terrain-model noise inflates total ascent by a third or more. Distances are great-circle sums over the resampled track.

Climbs were found by locating minima and maxima on the smoothed profile, discarding swings below 20 m of prominence, then keeping every rise of at least 400 m length, 40 m gain and 2.4% average. Categories use the standard climb score of metres gained × 100. Effort is a steady-power roll-out: gravity, rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag solved for speed segment by segment, with descents capped — it is a floor, not a prediction.

Place names, cols, summits and landmarks were matched against OpenStreetMap and checked against the tracks; the 2026 Tour de France stage figures quoted are the published race route, not this GPX.

The shared climb

Three of the four routes ride the same ascent out of Gavà towards Begues — the Côte de Begues of the Tour’s stage 2. The TDF26 recon turns off at the 406 m col; the two Garraf routes carry on over the top of the massif at 413 m. It is the biggest single climb on this page in all three.
